17. Analogue magnetic spatial sound

[MAGNETIC ANALOGUE SPACE: woody physical echoes, warm tape saturation, spring resonance, real room reflections, unstable magnetic decay, dusty analogue depth rather than clinically clean digital ambience]

Discover Suno’s vocabulary for our space.

18. Binson-style multi-head behaviour

[MULTI-HEAD MAGNETIC ECHO SOUND: one acoustic event produces several displaced magnetic repetitions with smoky physical decay and controlled feedback]

First describe the sound without relying entirely on the equipment name.

19. Saz creating dub-like chord space

[ANATOLIAN DUB SPACE: sparse heavy saz chord attacks bloom into multiple smoky magnetic echoes, creating deep dub-like spatial movement entirely from strings, amplifier and physical echo]

Explore how Suno translates the function without defaulting to synth dub stabs.

20. Three-note motif as musical DNA

[THREE-NOTE MUSICAL DNA: one simple recognisable three-note contour is the source of the entire composition and repeatedly returns in different sizes, instruments and densities]

Avoid note names initially so we can discover the conceptual terminology.

21. Literal three-note contour

[THREE-NOTE SEED: A4 → B-flat4 → G4, always preserving the same melodic contour when transformed]

Separate test for whether note specification changes Suno’s Style language.

22. Multiscale / fractal motif

23. Shorter–softer–brighter transformation law

[TRANSFORMATION RULE: every smaller generation of the motif becomes shorter, softer and brighter while keeping the same melodic contour]

This is one of the most important new composition rules, so test it alone.

24. Rainfall multiplication

[RAINFALL MULTIPLICATION: isolated musical droplets gradually reproduce into increasingly frequent smaller droplets until the musical space becomes densely filled]

Discover Suno terminology without telling it “fractal” first.

25. Rainfall macro-form

[RAINFALL ARRANGEMENT: isolated drops → gradual multiplication → increasing density → full downpour → sudden clearing → residual droplets → final solitary return]

See how Suno describes this as arrangement/form, not merely ambience.

26. Non-pop structural development

[EVOLVING FORM: no conventional verse-pre-chorus-chorus cycle; structure develops through accumulation, multiplication, density, clearing and return]

This helps us investigate how Suno names non-standard structure.

27. AMAN as vocal sound rather than lyrics

[AMAN VOCAL SOUND: intimate smoky female voice, breathy low-volume chest tone, AMAN beginning almost as a private breath and opening into a fragile sustained melodic phrase]

Keep this separate from Vocal House terminology initially.

28. AMAN as Anatolian melisma

[AMAN MELISMA: long soulful Anatolian melismatic AMAN, slow, restrained, intimate and emotionally suspended; longing, mercy, ache, memory and surrender]

Discover the vocal vocabulary Suno uses.

29. AMAN is not a vocal chop

[SUSTAINED VOCAL FORM: AMAN remains a long continuous melodic expression rather than rhythmic vocal chops, vocal stabs or sliced samples]

This directly tests one of Suno’s earlier substitutions.

[SHARED VOCAL-INSTRUMENT MOTIF: the female AMAN melisma and electric saz express the same three-note contour, behaving like two different scales or embodiments of one musical object]

That captures exactly what we were trying to describe perceptually. The listener should **feel** the 9/8 rather than hear a technical exercise.

The low end is also substantially better:

> **“davul-focused, deep and rounded with short physical impacts, wooden-body resonance and an extra end-of-cycle bloom”**

This time Suno did **not** convert our concept into synth sub + house kick. It retained:

**davul → physical impact → wooden resonance → end-of-cycle low-frequency event.**

Even better, it understood the reason for that final event:

> **“creates gravitational momentum instead of constant synthetic sub tone”**

That is essentially our pulse-9 concept expressed back to us in Suno's own language.

### The percussion interpretation is especially encouraging

This part is remarkably faithful:

> **“def and riq, smooth and continuous like elegant shakers and hi-hats yet clearly hand-played”**

and then:

> **“a subtle extra movement in the final three pulses that reveals the aksak lilt while preserving the trance”**

That's important.

It didn't merely identify **def/riq = house hats**. It retained both levels simultaneously:

**house-like continuous motion**  
+  
**culturally/rhythmically specific final 3-pulse Aksak behaviour**

That's precisely the fusion mechanism rather than merely the fusion *label*.

And darbuka:

> **“compact like acoustic house backbeats”**

Again, it understands **functional translation**, not substitution.

---

## Something else happened here

This was an **instrumental remix of the track already generated from the same prompt**.

So now Suno had two things available in the process:

1. our written description;
2. an existing musical generation embodying some interpretation of that description.

We should not claim from this alone exactly how Suno internally combines those inputs. But observationally, the resulting Style description is **much more specific to our rhythmic system** than its earlier text-only interpretations.

That makes this remix particularly valuable.

It is no longer merely saying:

> “Anatolian 9/8 Vocal House.”

It is describing **what makes this version of 9/8 Vocal House behave differently**.

---

## Compare the progression

**First test**

> Anatolian 9/8 → “stumbles then locks”  
> low end → kick/sub  
> atmosphere → Rhodes  
> vocal → chops

**Second test**

> “hypnotic uneven rolling pulse”  
> “organic acoustic low-end davul bass”  
> def/riq/darbuka  
> fuzzed saz  
> bowed strings

**Instrumental remix**

> four grounded anchors  
> final stretched return  
> asymmetry felt rather than counted  
> davul wooden-body resonance  
> end-cycle gravitational bloom  
> def/riq continuous house-like movement  
> final-three-pulse Aksak movement  
> hand-played microtiming  
> acoustic darbuka house-backbeat function

That is a clear progression toward the architecture we designed.

## And this gives us something we should preserve

Some of **Suno's own wording is actually better for describing the audible result** than some of our engineering language.

Particularly:

> **gentle asymmetrical sway**  
> **elastic circular feel**  
> **final stretched pull**  
> **end-of-cycle bloom**  
> **gravitational momentum**  
> **shimmering halo of def and riq**  
> **reveals the Aksak lilt while preserving the trance**

Those are excellent **sound-description phrases**.

They don't replace our technical instructions. They can sit *before* them:

**audible result:**  
“final stretched pull / gravitational momentum”

**construction:**  
davul anchors 1/3/5/7 + tuned resonance on pulse 9.

That is exactly the two-layer language we were looking for earlier.

### One thing I would not change yet

I would **not start rewriting the master prompt because this result looks good**.

We should preserve this generation and its Style description as a reference point. We're finally getting experimental evidence about which language resulted in the system preserving the unusual architecture.

The next useful comparison is the **actual remix audio**: whether what Suno describes here is genuinely audible—especially the 9/8 sway, final stretched pull, davul low-end behaviour and final-three-pulse percussion movement.

Because if the **audio does what this Style description says**, we have found something much more important than a good prompt: we have the beginning of a repeatable **sound grammar for the series**.

This is a very strong comparison because the **web lyrics-creation interpretation is conceptually aligned**, while the **app Create Style output is mostly genre substitution**.

The web version preserves the actual system unusually well:

- **“minimal, evolving, and self-similar”**
- **“one tiny three-note seed”**
- **“coming back in new shapes”**
- **“related but not duplicated”**
- **“early ideas stay audible”**
- **“later parts bend around them”**
- **“alive, inherited, and constantly adapting”**
- **“family of variations”**
- **“each return carrying the memory of everything that came before”**

That is probably the closest **complete Suno-native summary** we have seen so far. It captures identity, coexistence, inheritance, adaptation, and memory of prior layers without over-explaining the mechanics.

The app Style button, by contrast, largely ignores the compositional law and maps the text into a familiar package:

> intimate ambient indie ballad, 72 BPM, felt piano, nylon guitar, cello, brushed drums, tape saturation, synth pad...

That is not a reflection of the recursive architecture. It is a **stylistic completion guess**.

So I would now distinguish these two Suno behaviours very clearly:

- **Web lyrics-creation description** = much better at reflecting the **compositional concept**
- **App Create Style button** = much more likely to turn the concept into a **genre/instrument/production template**

The best Suno wording to preserve from this result is probably:

> **related but not duplicated**  
> **early ideas stay audible while later parts bend around them**  
> **alive, inherited, and constantly adapting**  
> **each return carrying the memory of everything that came before**

That last one is especially strong because it gives us a compact musical meaning for cumulative environment:

> **every new form carries the memory of prior forms.**

That may be a better working phrase than some of our more technical language.

Yes. That’s another useful observation from your testing.

What you’re describing is that Suno doesn’t only extract **content** from the Lyrics section; it also seems to adapt the **register and quality of its response** to how that content is written.

So if the Lyrics content is:

- technical and structured, the Lyricist tends to answer more analytically;
- sensory and evocative, it tends to answer more musically/descriptively;
- casual or vague, it may respond more generically;
- precise and concept-heavy, it can mirror that level of abstraction and sophistication.

That matters because it means the Lyrics section is doing two jobs at once:

> **it supplies the musical idea, and it sets the conversational frame for how Suno interprets that idea.**

So when we test Suno, we should be careful not only about **what terms we include**, but also **how we phrase them**.

That gives us another research variable:

**same concept, different register**
- plain descriptive language
- technical/compositional language
- sensory/metaphorical language
- concise directive language

Then compare whether the Lyricist and Style generator produce materially different interpretations.

That could tell us which wording style gives the most faithful translation without pushing Suno into generic genre completion.

Yes. The strongest version of this idea is **not** “Anatolian psych + six electronic genres.” That would dilute the identity. The electronic references should define **groove behaviour, spatial depth, pacing, and listener use-case**, while the audible material remains Anatolian/organic/analogue.

Your own Suno research also supports keeping the **headline genre vocabulary relatively focused** and moving detailed instructions into instrumentation, production and section-level commands; excessive genre/instrument stacking can cause Suno to discard priorities. fileciteturn0file2 The metatag research likewise supports section-specific emotional, structural and stylistic direction rather than putting everything into one undifferentiated style sentence. fileciteturn0file14

## 1. What I hear as the actual new genre

I would establish the series around:

### **Anatolian Aksak Deep Psych**

with a secondary descriptor:

**organic analogue nocturnal groove**

Not:

> Anatolian rock + trap + deep house + vocal house + nu disco + chillout + dub techno + downtempo

Instead:

> **1970s Anatolian psychedelic rock × organic deep-house architecture, in 9/8 Aksak**

Then borrow selectively:

| Reference language | What we take | What we do **not** take |
|---|---|---|
| Elegant Deep House | low-density arrangement, smooth low end, intimate vocals, long emotional arcs | generic polished house presets |
| Deep House | persistent hypnotic pulse, bass-led groove | standard 4/4 kick |
| Vocal House | close emotional vocal as focal point | oversized EDM chorus |
| Nu Disco | bass movement, rhythmic lift, sophistication | glossy disco strings/synths |
| Chillout | negative space, long decays, unhurried listening | sleepy ambient wash |
| Dub Techno | recursive echoes, depth, disappearing/reappearing motifs | digital chord stabs |
| Downtempo | restraint and body movement | beatless background music |
| Anatolian psych | saz, modal melody, fuzz, raw drums, hypnotism | retro pastiche |
| Acoustic trap | low/sub emphasis, sharp transient punctuation, sparse rhythmic space | trap hats, 808 kits, digital rolls |

That distinction matters enormously.

The first reference channel explicitly describes its own territory as **Deep House, Vocal House, Nu Disco and Chillout**, centred on smooth grooves, deep basslines, soulful vocals, intimate atmosphere and late-night/night-drive/focus listening. citeturn230516youtube19turn230516youtube20

The second channel, **Deep & Elegant**, is a substantial channel rather than a tiny reference account; third-party channel data currently lists roughly 112K subscribers and 158 videos. A preserved channel tracklist also shows long-form deep-house programming built from smooth, relatively restrained records rather than dramatic festival-style peaks. citeturn451301search0turn451301search1

So the useful lesson is **continuity and atmosphere**, not copying their production vocabulary.

---

# 2. The unique rule for this series

I would make this the series' non-negotiable sonic law:

> **Electronic behaviour, acoustic source.**

A deep-house pad becomes:

**bowed saz harmonics + harmonium/organ + room resonance → tape saturation → spring reverb**

A dub-techno delay becomes:

**real tape echo with feedback riding**

A sub synth becomes:

**low davul + muted electric bass / baritone saz resonance → tape compression**

A synthetic shaker becomes:

**def/riq skin and jingles recorded close and overdubbed**

A riser becomes:

**feedbacking fuzzed saz harmonic gradually opened with an analogue wah/filter pedal**

A house sidechain pump becomes:

**performance dynamics, compressor keyed from davul if hardware is available, or manually ridden ensemble breathing**

This gives us something potentially recognisable after only several tracks.

Not “retro Anatolian house.”

More like:

### **music that behaves electronically without being electronically generated.**

That is a much stronger artistic proposition.

---

# 3. The three-note fractal motif should become the DNA

This part is particularly strong because it connects directly to the genuine multiscale/fractal composition principle we established before: the seed should generate **microstructure, rhythm, phrasing, sections and macro-form**, rather than merely being repeated decoratively.

Let the seed be:

**A → B → C**

The pitches do not need to be specified yet. The critical property is its **contour**.

For example:

**low → high → middle**

Every descendant preserves:

**low → high → middle**

but changes three variables simultaneously:

- **shorter**
- **softer**
- **brighter**

So:

### Generation 0 — Seed
Three heavy fuzz-saz notes.

Large.

Dry.

Almost alone.

### Generation 1
Same three-note contour.

Half the duration.

Lower volume.

Played higher or nearer the saz bridge.

### Generation 2
Again half-sized.

Quieter.

Riq/saz harmonic doubles the contour.

### Generation 3
Tiny fragments.

Almost droplets.

Pick noise, string harmonics and rim-like darbuka articulation carry the same contour.

Now the listener is effectively **zooming into the original three notes**.

That is fractal composition rather than ordinary motivic repetition.

---

# 4. Let the 9/8 rhythm undergo the same recursion

I would use:

## **9/8 = 2 + 2 + 2 + 3**

Count:

**1-2 | 3-4 | 5-6 | 7-8-9**

This gives us the asymmetrical Anatolian body movement.

But we should create a deep-house *continuity illusion* inside it.

### Low pulse

**DAVUL**

strong:

**1 — 3 — 5 — 7**

with the final three-unit cell carrying the asymmetry.

So the listener gets:

**BOOM — BOOM — BOOM — BOOM-da-da**

rather than a folk-dance demonstration of 9/8.

### Darbuka

Sharp counterhits around:

**2 / 4 / 6 / 8-9**

### Def / riq

Provides the high-frequency continuum.

Not trap hi-hats.

Instead:

> progressively finer riq rolls occupying the spaces produced by the motif recursion.

This is where your **“acoustic trap”** concept becomes convincing.

Trap contributes its **hierarchy**:

- enormous low transient,
- dry sharp backbeat,
- tiny accelerated upper percussion,
- negative space.

But every sound is physical.

---

# 5. Rainfall is the arrangement model

The arrangement should not grow conventionally as:

> intro → verse → chorus → big drop

It should behave like a storm system.

### **Phase I — First Drop**
0:00–0:25

One three-note saz motif.

Tape hiss.

Room.

A single davul resonance eventually appears.

Female vocal either absent or one breath/word.

No full groove yet.

---

### **Phase II — Isolated Rain**
0:25–0:55

Motif repeats.

Second occurrence is shorter/softer/brighter.

Then another.

Distances between events contract.

Small darbuka responses begin.

The listener discovers the 9/8 implicitly.

---

### **Phase III — Pattern Recognition**
0:55–1:30

Bass enters.

Not huge.

Warm, round and repetitive.

Def/riq creates a continuous upper pulse.

Now something similar to elegant deep house emerges — **without changing the instrument language**.

The groove should feel:

> sophisticated, nocturnal, hypnotic, bodily.

---

### **Phase IV — Rainfall**
1:30–2:05

Female vocal enters fully.

Three-note instrumental motif continues under her but becomes less obvious.

Her phrase ending produces:

**voice**

→ two tape echoes

→ each echo creates two shorter descendants

so perceptually:

**1 → 2 → 4**

The descendants become:

- quieter,
- shorter,
- brighter,
- farther into the stereo/room field.

This is excellent because the **vocal delay itself follows the compositional law**.

---

### **Phase V — Downpour**
2:05–2:40

Heavy fuzz electric saz finally occupies the foreground.

Do **not** make it a generic rock solo.

Its improvisation should be derived from the three-note seed.

Davul gets deeper.

Bass becomes slightly more melodic.

Riq recursion becomes dense.

Female harmonies appear only as fragments.

This is the maximum density point.

---

### **Phase VI — Dub Dissolution**
2:40–3:15

Instead of an EDM breakdown:

instruments disappear one at a time.

Tape echo remains.

Saz chord → echo.

Darbuka hit → room.

Voice fragment → 2 → 4 echoes.

The track effectively dissolves into its descendants.

This imports **dub techno's spatial thinking** without importing dub-techno synthesis.

---

### **Phase VII — Second Rain**
3:15–3:50

Groove returns, but transformed.

The original three-note motif now appears simultaneously at:

- slow scale — bass/saz
- medium scale — guitar/saz
- fast scale — percussion
- micro scale — vocal echo

This should be the compositional payoff.

The listener may not consciously recognise why everything suddenly feels unified.

But everything is the same object at different magnifications.

---

### **Phase VIII — Last Drop**
3:50–end

Strip everything away.

The exact original three-note phrase returns.

But now perhaps:

**three clean acoustic saz notes**

instead of fuzz.

Then:

one tiny vocal echo.

Tape hiss.

Stop.

That gives the entire track:

**seed → multiplication → saturation → dissolution → transformed return.**

That is the series' first serious signature.

---

# 6. Vocal character

Do **not** request a huge “soulful house diva.”

Wrong world.

I would use:

### Lead

**intimate raw female contralto / low mezzo**

Characteristics:

- close microphone
- audible breath
- slight chest texture
- restrained ornamentation
- conversational verses
- occasional Anatolian melismatic turns
- no polished belting
- no pitch-perfect glossy tone
- no autotune
- small inconsistencies retained
- almost uncomfortable closeness

The voice should sit **inside the groove**, not above it.

For the late-night reference audience this is more interesting than another highly polished vocal-house singer.

---

# 7. Analogue spatial design

This is where we can convert deep-house luxury into something far more authentic.

### **Foreground**
dry intimate vocal  
sharp darbuka  
saz pick transient

### **Middle field**
electric bass  
davul body  
Rhodes/organ if used  
rhythm saz

### **Far field**
spring reverb  
room microphones  
tape repeats  
feedbacking harmonics

Instead of constructing space with huge digital reverbs:

record **distance**.

For example:

- vocal mic at 10–20 cm
- room mic several metres away
- saz amplifier close-mic + corridor mic
- percussion mic at chest level plus room
- re-amp vocal echoes through a guitar amplifier into an actual room

Now depth exists acoustically before effects.

---

# 8. Analogue-only effects vocabulary

Use:

**tape saturation**  
**reel-to-reel slapback**  
**tape feedback delay**  
**spring reverb**  
**plate reverb if physically available**  
**tube/transformer distortion**  
**fuzz pedal**  
**wah pedal**  
**analogue tremolo**  
**analogue phaser**  
**real room reflections**  
**speaker re-amping**  
**mic movement**  
**tape varispeed**

Avoid:

**digital synths**  
**virtual pads**  
**EDM supersaws**  
**software arpeggiators as the sonic source**  
**808 samples**  
**trap sample packs**  
**digital risers**  
**granular plugins**  
**autotune**  
**hyper-clean limiting**

Even the “brightness progression” can be produced physically:

first motif = neck pickup / darker mic position  
second = bridge pickup  
third = brighter pick position  
fourth = natural harmonic / small metallic percussion doubling.

That is far more convincing than an automated digital filter.

---

# 9. Bass is crucial for playlist compatibility

The bass should probably be the bridge between the two worlds.

Not an aggressive psych-rock bass.

Not a generic deep-house sub.

Use:

### **deep muted electric bass + davul resonance**

Warm.

Very repetitive.

Slightly syncopated.

Melodic movement only at structural boundaries.

This gives the **home / car / work / late-night** usability you want.

The references repeatedly position this type of music around night drives, relaxing, focus and intimate listening. citeturn230516youtube19turn230516youtube20

The more radical material can therefore happen **above the bass** while the low-frequency foundation remains reassuring.

---

# 10. Playlist compatibility without becoming generic

I would impose five constraints:

1. **Recognisable groove inside 15–25 seconds.**
2. **Lead vocal or unmistakable melodic identity before ~60 seconds.**
3. **No harsh frequency wall despite heavy fuzz.**
4. **One dominant motif listeners can retain after one play.**
5. **Continuous micro-change without obvious EDM drops.**

Your older production research reached a related conclusion: groove-oriented arrangements benefit from ongoing small changes rather than static looping, and organic feel comes from microtiming, dynamics and human imperfection. fileciteturn0file6

Here, however, we should adapt that principle to the **9/8 recursive rainfall architecture**, rather than importing the earlier 4/4 nu-disco formula.

---

# 11. What I would deliberately NOT use

This is important.

I would exclude:

> generic deep house  
> tropical house  
> EDM drops  
> four-on-the-floor 4/4  
> trap hi-hats  
> 808 drum machine  
> digital synth pads  
> supersaws  
> glossy nu-disco strings  
> festival risers  
> pitch-corrected vocals  
> quantized percussion  
> cinematic trailer drums  
> generic “ethnic” ornamentation  
> overproduced world-music fusion  
> lounge saxophone  
> lo-fi beat clichés

Especially **“ethnic.”**

We know exactly what the musical system is.

Call it **Anatolian**, **Aksak**, **electric saz**, **davul**, **darbuka**, **def**, **riq**.

---

# 12. First working Suno genre architecture

Because Suno can lose priority when overloaded, I would **not** give it all seven genres as equal labels. fileciteturn0file0

Instead:

```text
genre: [anatolian psychedelic rock / organic deep house]

rhythmic identity: [9/8 aksak 2+2+2+3, acoustic trap-derived dynamics, hypnotic asymmetrical dance groove]

mood: [nocturnal, intimate, hypnotic, earthy, sensual, mysterious, sophisticated]

sonic philosophy: [electronic behaviour created entirely from acoustic and analogue sources]
```

Then specify the reference genres as **behaviour**:

```text
arrangement influence: [deep-house continuity, vocal-house intimacy, nu-disco bass movement, chillout negative space, dub-techno recursive depth, downtempo restraint]
```

That is substantially safer and more precise than asking Suno to hybridise seven separate genres.

---

# 13. The central production command

If I had to reduce the whole project to one sentence for Suno, it would be:

> **A 9/8 Anatolian psychedelic nocturnal groove in which a three-note seed recursively multiplies like rainfall across saz, percussion, bass and female vocal tape echoes, using deep-house spatial and arrangement logic but absolutely no digital synthesis.**

That sentence contains the identity.

Everything else should support it.

---

## And I think we should make one further decision for Track 1

The **three-note motif should become the sonic logo of the entire series**.

Not necessarily the same notes in every song.

The **rule** remains:

**three-note seed → recursive descendants → altered scale → transformation → return.**

Track 1 introduces it through **rainfall**.

A later track could interpret it as breath, traffic, heartbeat, footsteps, waves, machinery, crowds, etc.

Then we are not simply creating an unusual song.

We are establishing a **compositional language for the project**. memcite

Yes — it **supports** that point quite strongly.

What I said was that the **Simple Creation description box is not the same test environment as Advanced/Custom Lyrics → Create Style**, because Simple Creation is more generative: it can interpret your prose as a broad song brief, then fill in missing implementation details itself.

And that is exactly what happened in **Output 2**.

It understood the abstract mechanism unusually well:

- recursive fragmentation,
- shorter / softer / brighter descendants,
- self-similar polyphony,
- non-conventional repetition,

but then it also **invented the production solution**:

- granular delay,
- convolution reverb,
- bowed glass,
- prepared piano,
- modular pulses,
- sub-bass drone.

So the Simple section seems useful for:

> **“What musical concept does Suno think this description implies?”**

but it is less clean for:

> **“What exact Style description does Suno derive from my text without adding its own arrangement/production ideas?”**

That distinction is now supported by your actual test results.

So going forward I’d separate them:

**Advanced/Custom Lyrics → Create Style** = interpretation probe  
**Simple Creation description** = interpretation + generative completion probe

Both are useful, but they answer different research questions.

Yes. Below is the **Suno-ready TXT version**, preserving the production architecture rather than compressing it into a generic style prompt. I have also preserved the technical corrections already established in the working record: 96-bar target, asymmetrical 9/8 house illusion, pulse-9 low boom, restrained def/riq fingerprint, bowed saz courses rather than impossible bowed chords, Binson-style magnetic drum echo, and physical rather than digital brightness changes. fileciteturn8file1 fileciteturn8file2

~~~writing id="aksak-vocal-house-track-1"
title: [untitled — track 1]

genre: [1970s anatolian psychedelic rock / underground elegant vocal house]

rhythmic identity: [120 bpm house pulse inside 9/8 aksak, grouped 2+2+2+3, asymmetrical four-anchor house illusion]

mood: [nocturnal, intimate, hypnotic, earthy, soulful, mysterious, sophisticated, emotionally restrained]

sonic philosophy: [electronic behaviour created entirely from acoustic and analogue sources]

vocal style: [intimate raw female contralto or low mezzo, breathy close-miked low-volume chest voice, almost whispered onset opening into fragile sustained melodic tone, restrained anatolian melisma, audible breath and natural pitch imperfections, no polished belting, no autotune]

vocal code: [AMAN only as the principal melismatic vocal object, with very minimal additional lyrics if any]

Begin from one recognisable three-note melodic seed.

Preserve the same recognisable three-note ancestry across different time scales.

The original strict recursive behaviour may be perceived as:

one source

negative space

deep
repetitive
slightly syncopated

This is identifying the problem what do you think? “
Why it’s turning into ambient

Ambient music relies on slow, soft, overlapping patterns that don’t change much — exactly what you get when you do “pure fractal”:

• Same shape repeated → similar notes, similar intervals, similar moods

• No sharp contrasts, no “surprises”

• Notes overlap and blend → washes of sound

• Slow repetition = ambient’s signature

Fractals naturally produce smooth, self-similar consistency — which is ambient’s core!
How fractals show up without sounding ambient

You just need to add contrast, rhythm, and structural “edges”:

1. Vary the “zoom speed” (change how fast patterns repeat)

• Ambient: slow, steady pace, same rhythm everywhere

• Fix: fast patterns in high register + slow in low register at the same time

• Example: quick notes up high, solid slow chords down low — same fractal shape, different speeds = texture, not wash

2. Change interval “density”

• Ambient: mostly 3rds & 5ths (soft, stable intervals)

• Fix: mix in sharper intervals — 2nds, 7ths, even tritones — at different levels

• Keep the fractal structure but alter the “sharpness” at different scales

3. Add rhythm & pulse (the biggest difference!)

• Ambient: little or no beat; floating

• Fix: apply your fractal pattern to rhythm too — not just pitches

◦ Main beat: pattern A

◦ Sub-beat: pattern A compressed

◦ Fills: pattern A faster

• Same shape, but timing gives it drive

4. Control “layers”

• Ambient: all layers active all the time → thick blur

• Fix: bring layers in/out, emphasize different levels at different times

• Start simple → add complexity → pull back — dynamic structure
Quick example

Your base fractal unit: C→E→G

• Ambient way: all 3, plus their triads, all playing slow & long together

• Your way:

◦ Bass: C (steady beat)

◦ Chord: E→G changing on beat 3

◦ Melody: C→E→G→E→C fast & crisp

• Same fractal DNA — completely different sound
In short

Fractal = the pattern relationship, not the tempo or softness. It’s like a fractal tree: same branching shape, but you can make it a delicate fern (ambient) or a jagged pine with sharp branches and strong trunk (our style).”

A dark, warm, late-night groove with the physical depth and hypnotic repetition of underground Vocal House, but carried by the uneven rolling movement of Anatolian 9/8 Aksak rhythm.

The sound should feel smooth and immediately bodily, never awkward or mathematically complex. The asymmetry is felt as a gentle pull, stretch and return rather than as an obvious odd-meter exercise.

The music is deep, elegant, raw and intimate. Heavy acoustic low frequencies sit beneath dry hand percussion, fuzzed electric saz, sustained bowed-string atmosphere and a close soulful female voice.

The production feels analogue, woody, dusty, magnetic and human. Nothing should sound clinically electronic or digitally perfect.

[RHYTHMIC SOUND]

The groove feels like a steady late-night house pulse that subtly loses its symmetry at the end of every cycle.

Four strong low-frequency anchors create familiarity and forward motion.

After the fourth anchor, the rhythm stretches slightly longer before returning to the first beat.

This final stretch creates the distinctive Aksak sway.

The listener should be able to move naturally to the groove without needing to consciously count 9/8.

The rhythm should feel hypnotic, elastic and circular rather than broken or irregular.

[LOW-END SOUND]

The low end is deep, warm, rounded and physical.

It should resemble the weight of a sophisticated underground house kick and sub system, but its character remains acoustic and organic.

Each davul strike has a short physical impact followed by a warm wooden-body resonance.

At the end of the rhythmic cycle, an additional deep resonance creates a gravitational pull into the next downbeat.

The low end breathes between impacts rather than creating a constant synthetic bass tone.

[HIGH-PERCUSSION SOUND]

The upper percussion forms a fine shimmering layer around the heavy davul pulse.

Def and riq should feel smooth, restrained and continuous, similar in rhythmic function to an elegant house shaker and hi-hat groove, but clearly produced by skins, fingers and small metal jingles.

The sound is crisp but never brittle.

Tiny timing and dynamic differences keep the pattern alive.

Inside the final three-pulse part of the Aksak cycle, the percussion makes a subtle extra movement that reveals the asymmetry without disturbing the hypnotic flow.

[DARBUKA SOUND]

The darbuka is dry, sharp and close.

Its attacks behave like compact house backbeats without imitating an electronic snare.

The sound should be short, dampened and tactile, with very little tail.

It punctuates the groove rather than dominating it.

[ELECTRIC SAZ SOUND]

The lead saz is dark, woody, slightly dangerous and emotionally expressive.

Heavy vintage fuzz thickens the strings but does not erase the natural pick attack, bends or Anatolian ornamentation.

The sound sits between raw 1970s psychedelic amplification and a refined nocturnal lead instrument.

It should never resemble a generic distorted electric guitar.

[BOWED SAZ ATMOSPHERE]

Behind the groove is a wide, slow-moving cloud of sustained string resonance.

The texture should perform the emotional role normally associated with a lush deep-house pad, but it must sound organic, unstable and physically generated.

Individual bowed saz tones overlap and breathe against one another.

Small tuning differences create movement.

The result is warm, ghostly, slightly weeping and continuously changing rather than smooth and synthetic.

[THREE-NOTE MOTIF SOUND]

A simple three-note melodic shape is the recognisable DNA of the track.

The first version is large, slow and exposed.

Later versions sound like progressively smaller reflections of the same phrase.

As the motif becomes smaller, it becomes shorter, quieter and brighter.

The listener should hear the same melodic shape at different magnifications, like repeatedly zooming into one musical object.

[RAINDROP SOUND]

The smallest versions of the motif resemble tiny bright droplets.

They are brief, delicate and high in register.

They may appear as short saz harmonics, fine string attacks or similarly physical acoustic details.

They should not sound like electronic arpeggiators or digital effects.

The impression is of rain gradually multiplying around the main groove.

[VOCAL SOUND]

The female voice is extremely close, smoky, breathy and emotionally restrained.

It begins almost as a private breath and then opens into a fragile sustained pitch.

The performance feels human and slightly imperfect.

AMAN is not shouted and is not used as a conventional house vocal sample.

It should sound like a private late-night expression of longing carried slowly across the groove.

[VOCAL ECHO SOUND]

After selected AMAN phrases, the voice leaves behind small acoustic and magnetic reflections.

The first echoes remain recognisably connected to the original voice.

Later descendants become shorter, quieter, thinner and brighter.

Yes. **This is the point where the interpretation became structurally correct.**

What changed here was deeper than just fixing the genre list.

In this response, the project finally stopped being treated as **“How do we make Track 1?”** and started being treated as **“How do we build a music brand and catalogue system?”**

The key shift was:

> **Gentleman = broad creator/tastemaker brand**  
> **Deep & Elegant = narrower, highly legible listening/product brand**

That distinction directly maps onto what you are trying to build.

The important insight was not simply that Gentleman uses more genres. It was that **breadth and focus can coexist inside one ecosystem**:

- the umbrella identity allows experimentation and genre movement;
- the focused identity gives listeners a reliable emotional/sonic destination;
- both reinforce the same catalogue and label ecosystem;
- the audience learns the creator’s taste, while also having a predictable format they can return to.

That is much closer to your original intention.

And this section is particularly important:

> “Those phrases create permission for variation.”

That is exactly what your genre list was doing in the original prompt. You were not saying:

> “Put all these genres into Track 1.”

You were defining the **creative territory that the brand is allowed to travel through**.

So the actual progression was:

**First answer:**  
I incorrectly narrowed your idea into one proposed hybrid sound.

**Second answer:**  
I corrected it to a series with different genre centres.

**After studying Gentleman / Deep & Elegant properly:**  
I understood that the real model is an **ecosystem**: broad creative freedom + recognisable brand promise + focused audience positioning + catalogue consistency.

That third understanding is the one we should carry forward.

And there is one further consequence: we should **not freeze the brand DNA too narrowly yet**.

For example, saying the entire brand must always have 9/8, fuzz saz, recursive three-note motifs, female vocals, or rainfall architecture would repeat my original mistake. Those belong to **Track 1 unless we later deliberately promote one of them into a recurring signature**.

The permanent brand layer should initially be broader:

> **Anatolian-rooted, analogue/acoustic, emotionally atmospheric, sophisticated, alternative, groove-conscious, human, timeless — with freedom to move through the genre territories you specified.**

Then each release gets its own musical proposition.

That is the framework I would now use.

For this **first interpretation test**, I’d keep custom settings as neutral as possible so they don’t contaminate what we’re actually measuring.

Use:

- **Instrumental:** off, because this first test is explicitly about a sustained vocal tone.
- **Weirdness:** default / middle position.
- **Style Influence:** default / middle position.
- **Exclude Styles:** leave blank for the first pass.
- **Persona:** none.
- **Reference audio / uploaded audio:** none.
- **Lyrics mode:** Custom, with only the test instruction in square brackets.
- **Style field:** leave empty, then use **Create Style** from the Lyrics content.
- **Title:** either blank or something neutral like `test 01 recursive vocal` if Suno requires one.

Most importantly, across your **three accounts**, keep every controllable setting identical. We want:

> **same input + same settings → compare Suno’s interpretation**

not three slightly different experiments.

I’d also avoid changing Weirdness or Style Influence between accounts on Test 1. Once we know how the baseline interpretation behaves, **then** we can deliberately test whether those controls alter the interpretation or only the generated audio.

For the first test, paste only:

```text
[A single sustained vocal tone recursively generates smaller reflections of itself. Each new reflection preserves the identity of its parent but becomes shorter, softer, brighter, and more distant in space. The process repeats over multiple scales, creating self-similar vocal architecture rather than a conventional echo. The music evolves through recursive inheritance instead of repetition.]
```

Then **Create Style**, and save the exact result from Account 1, Account 2 and Account 3 before generating anything.

I checked them. Your wording in the original prompt was already pointing in the right direction; I misread the role of the references.

The important distinction is:

> **We are not copying their music. We are studying why their channel/brand works, then applying those success principles to our own original sonic identity.**

And yes, the second reference in particular has already crossed the scale you were talking about. **Deep & Elegant** is currently reported at roughly **117K subscribers, 30.5M views and 180 videos**; an earlier Social Blade snapshot showed 112K subscribers and 27M views. citeturn185357search1turn185357search0

The first channel, **Elegant Deep House**, is smaller but still has very strong individual-video performance. Recent examples include about **394K views** on *Best Mix Hits 2026*, about **204K** on *Lonely Love*, and about **166K** on *Don't Leave Me*. citeturn296288youtube0turn939885youtube37turn939885youtube36

So there is absolutely something worth reverse-engineering here.

## What they are actually doing correctly

The first major thing is that they are not merely selling **genre**.

They are selling a **repeatable emotional environment**.

Elegant Deep House repeatedly frames its music around:

**late nights  
night drives  
city lights  
relaxation  
focus  
romantic/intimate listening  
emotional reflection**

And the music vocabulary stays remarkably consistent:

**deep basslines  
soft/soulful vocals  
smooth grooves  
atmospheric melodies  
minimal/elegant production  
emotional depth**

Their own descriptions explicitly position the channel as combining modern house rhythms with a **timeless, minimal aesthetic** and targeting those exact listening contexts. citeturn296288youtube0turn296288youtube1

That is not accidental SEO language. It is their **brand architecture**.

And this connects directly to what you wrote:

> late nights, night drives, relaxation, focus, home, car, or work listening

You were already identifying their strategy correctly.

---

## Deep & Elegant is even more instructive

This channel is much more than somebody uploading random deep-house mixes.

Their channel identity is built around **Gentleman** and a coherent label ecosystem. Current channel information describes the tracks as being released through the **GNTLMN** label. citeturn185357search1

Their titles repeatedly use vocabulary like:

**Elegant  
Midnight  
Luxury  
Deep  
Vibes  
Night  
Liquid  
Pure  
Grooves**

There is extremely strong semantic consistency.

Examples include titles such as:

- *Midnight House Grooves*
- *Luxury Vibes*
- *Pure Deep House*
- *Midnight Drive*
- *Liquid Dreams*
- *Deep Elegant*

This means the listener learns the channel **before hearing the next record**.

That is branding.

---

# They are also remarkably disciplined musically

A documented Deep & Elegant tracklist runs approximately 50 minutes and contains ten tracks at roughly five-minute intervals. citeturn185357search2

That indicates another important principle:

### They do not exhaust the listener.

The music maintains a relatively narrow emotional bandwidth while providing continuous microvariation.

That matters enormously for:

- repeat listening
- work listening
- driving
- background listening
- long-session retention
- playlists

The listener is not being attacked by a new concept every thirty seconds.

Instead:

> **stable world + continuous subtle variation**

That principle should absolutely become part of our brand.

---

# And there is evidence of the listener response we want

The comments around Deep & Elegant are very revealing.

Listeners describe using the music:

- after work
- late Saturday night
- with coffee
- to relax when stressed
- during travel
- for summer/sunset atmosphere

One comment specifically describes the music as transporting them to a **summer beach-bar sunset**; another says they were stressed, started listening, and immediately relaxed. citeturn185357search2

This is important because they have managed to create:

> **music with identity that does not demand exclusive attention.**

That is precisely the difficult territory your prompt describes.

---

# So our objective becomes much clearer

We should follow their **business/music-design logic**:

### 1. A clearly recognisable sonic world

But ours is:

**analogue Anatolian / organic / raw / sophisticated**

rather than conventional electronic deep house.

---

### 2. A recognisable listening use-case

Our brand should immediately imply:

**night drive  
late night  
after work  
home listening  
focus  
intimate space  
urban solitude  
slow movement**

Not necessarily stated identically every time, but consistently encoded into the music and presentation.

---

### 3. Consistency without identical songs

This is crucial.

Deep & Elegant can move through different producers and tracks while preserving a coherent channel identity.

Our equivalent should be:

## fixed brand DNA + changing genre emphasis

So your original list makes much more sense:

**Anatolian rock  
trap  
deep house  
vocal house  
nu disco  
chillout  
dub techno  
downtempo**

Those are our **creative territories**.

Each track explores a different intersection.

For example:

| Track | Dominant intersection |
|---|---|
| 01 | Anatolian psych × acoustic trap |
| 02 | Anatolian psych × deep house |
| 03 | Anatolian soul × vocal house |
| 04 | Anatolian groove × nu disco |
| 05 | Anatolian acoustic × chillout |
| 06 | Anatolian psych × dub techno architecture |
| 07 | Anatolian folk textures × downtempo |
| 08 | selected synthesis of earlier identities |

But every one still carries the same underlying brand DNA.

That is what I should have extracted from your prompt initially.

---

# Our shared brand DNA

I would currently define it as six permanent rules.

### **1. Anatolian root**

Saz/bağlama language, modal melodic thinking, Aksak possibilities, Anatolian percussion and the emotional vocabulary of Anatolian music.

Not necessarily all instruments in every record.

But the **musical ancestry stays audible**.

### **2. Analogue/acoustic source philosophy**

This may become our most differentiating feature.

Electronic genres teach us **what sounds should do**.

They do not dictate **what produces those sounds**.

So:

deep-house pad → acoustic/analogue sustained texture  
dub delay → tape echo  
trap hats → riq/def subdivision  
sub → bass guitar/davul/body resonance  
filter sweep → wah/analogue filter/mic movement  
digital ambience → room/spring/plate/tape

### **3. Human imperfection**

No antiseptic AI sheen.

Microtiming.

String noise.

Breath.

Skin.

Tape.

Room.

Dynamic variation.

The previous research you uploaded repeatedly emphasised that humanisation and subtle evolution are central to successful groove-based production. fileciteturn0file6

### **4. Sophisticated low-frequency groove**

This is probably what connects us most strongly to the reference audience.

The bass cannot become folk accompaniment.

It needs to be one of the main reasons people keep listening.

Smooth.

Physical.

Repetitive enough to hypnotise.

Interesting enough to reward headphones.

### **5. Emotional intimacy**

The references succeed partly because the emotional scale is **personal rather than theatrical**.

So our vocals should generally avoid:

huge pop belting  
overdramatic theatricality  
generic “world music” performance

and instead favour:

close-mic  
restrained  
raw  
sensual  
fragile  
conversational  
occasionally intense

### **6. Long-form atmosphere**

Even if we eventually release individual songs rather than only hour-long mixes, the tracks need to **flow naturally into one another**.

That is another major brand opportunity.

Eventually the album/playlist should feel like one continuous environment.

---

# There is another thing they understand extremely well: naming

Look at the repeated semantic field:

**Midnight  
Elegant  
Luxury  
Liquid  
Deep  
Night  
Feeling  
Love  
Lonely  
Vibes**

They aren't trying to explain music theory in the title.

They sell an **emotional scene**.

Our equivalent probably shouldn't be:

> “9/8 Anatolian Fractal Psych Trap”

as the public-facing title.

That can describe the production internally.

The public presentation should probably live in a vocabulary more like:

**Rain on Stone  
After Midnight  
Copper Rain  
The Last Light  
Dust After Dark  
Red Window  
Quiet Fire  
Under the Bosphorus  
Night Crossing**

Not proposing these as final titles; I'm showing the branding principle.

**Technical complexity inside. Simple emotional image outside.**

That is exactly what these channels do effectively.

---

# Where we can potentially outperform the format creatively

Their consistency is a strength, but it can also create interchangeability.

Our opportunity is:

> **retain their usability and consistency while introducing actual compositional identity.**

That's where your recursive/fractal idea becomes very valuable.

The three-note rainfall motif is not merely an experimental flourish.

It can solve the exact branding problem:

listeners receive something:

**smooth enough to live with**

but underneath it:

**musically sophisticated enough to discover repeatedly.**

So Track 1 can already establish:

- three-note seed
- multiscale recursion
- rainfall arrangement
- 9/8 Aksak
- physical analogue/acoustic sound
- intimate female voice
- fuzz saz
- sophisticated bass
- large negative space
- dub-derived depth

while remaining comfortable enough for an hour-long playlist environment.

That is substantially more interesting than simply recreating their Deep House formula.

---

## One correction to my previous answer

I previously suggested:

> “Recognisable groove inside 15–25 seconds.”

That was too prescriptive.

After looking more carefully at what you're actually building, I wouldn't impose normal streaming-pop optimisation on every song.

The better brand rule is:

> **The sonic world must be recognisable immediately; the full groove can reveal itself gradually.**

That distinction is important.

Track 1 could therefore start with the isolated three-note rainfall seed and still belong perfectly to the brand before the bass even arrives.

---

## The actual project proposition now looks much sharper

I would phrase it internally as:

> **Take the sophisticated, emotionally functional, repeat-listenable ecosystem pioneered by channels such as Deep & Elegant and Elegant Deep House, preserve what makes that audience return—continuity, low-frequency warmth, atmosphere, intimacy, elegant restraint and lifestyle compatibility—but replace the conventional electronic vocabulary with a distinctive Anatolian analogue/acoustic musical language. Each release explores a different intersection of Anatolian rock, trap, deep house, vocal house, nu disco, chillout, dub techno and downtempo while preserving the same core sonic identity.**

That is what your original prompt was describing.

And now that I've actually checked the references, I would **not simplify the vision**. The individual details you gave—playlist context, alternative audience, emotional depth, home/car/work listening, analogue-only reinterpretation, experimentation, authenticity, uniqueness—are not unnecessary wording.

They are different parts of the brand strategy.

We should preserve them. memcite

parts.text: Sure, let me take a look. Yeah, so looking at the last turn or two, I think the shift we were circling around was from math to perceptible sound behavior. So instead of asking for a numerical result, say what the listener should feel, something that grows and multiplies organically. And reading your text, I think I'd push that even further. Don't think of it as a fractal math problem; think of it as a sound family tree. Every new event should feel like it has a parent. It inherits a shape but changes scale. For example, the parent is a dark, long saz note. The child is the same contour at half duration, softer and slightly brighter, and the grandchild's a harmonic or a percussive flick that still traces the same contour. I think the listener only has to feel inheritance, not the counting. And then apply that across dimensions: rhythm fills space gradually, timbre shifts from dark to bright, register or space or echoes generate smaller echoes. That way the model isn't solving a puzzle; it's following inheritance rules.

Glass crack's a great one. Uh, the seed is a single sharp fracture. The environment is tension in the glass. The child events are branching hairline cracks, like finer, quieter, but multiplied, spreading until the whole pane sings with stress. Uh, if rain is about gentle multiplication, glass is about brittle inevitability. Same rule, but a totally different poem.

parts:
This is a very clean result, and it confirms the split we’ve been seeing between **Lyrics Edit interpretation** and **Create Style generation**.

## Lyrics section response

> “Warm, looping, and a little cerebral, it keeps the same melody shape while every new layer bends under what came before.”

This is **conceptually strong**.

It preserves:

- **same melody shape** → inherited identity
- **every new layer bends under what came before** → environment-dependent adaptation
- cumulative change rather than pure copying

The only weak word is:

> **“looping”**

That is not quite our concept. We are explicitly trying to avoid ordinary looping. But the rest of the sentence is excellent.

The strongest phrase here is:

> **“every new layer bends under what came before”**

That is probably one of the best concise formulations we have found so far.

---

## Create Style button response

> “Warm cerebral art-pop, looping minimalist pop, evolving layered arrangement, repetitive melodic motif…”

This is much weaker conceptually.

It converts the abstract rule into a familiar stylistic package:

- art-pop
- minimalist pop
- repetitive motif
- tape keys
- analog synth bass
- muted guitar
- granular vocal fragments
- drum-machine groove

So again:

### Lyrics Edit
**understands the compositional rule**

### Create Style
**translates the rule into a genre/production guess**

That difference is becoming quite consistent in your tests.

---

## What I’d record from this test

### Preserved well
- same melodic identity
- cumulative influence
- later layers shaped by earlier ones

### Normalised
- “looping”
- “repetitive melodic motif”
- “minimalist pop”

### Invented implementation
- tape-saturated keys
- synth bass
- muted electric guitar
- granular vocals
- filter sweeps
- drum machine
- distortion

### Useful Suno wording
Keep these:

> **same melody shape**

> **every new layer bends under what came before**

That second phrase is especially valuable because it expresses the dynamic rule with almost no technical jargon.

## Current best compact formulation

I’d now write our core rule as:

> **The same musical identity returns in new forms, and every new layer bends under what came before.**

That is much cleaner than the earlier over-engineered explanation.

If I were a **normal Suno user** trying to make one song, I’d split my input by **what must happen exactly** versus **what I’m happy for Suno to interpret globally**.

| Input | Where I’d put it | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Actual words to be sung | **Lyrics** | Exact lyrical content belongs here. |
| Verse / chorus / bridge / intro / outro positions | **Lyrics** | These are positional instructions: *where* something happens. |
| Vocal event at a specific moment | **Lyrics** | `[whispered]`, `[spoken]`, `[layered harmony]`, `[long melisma]`, etc. are local instructions. |
| Instrument enters/stops at a specific section | **Lyrics** | If I specifically want saz to enter after verse 1, I place that instruction there. |
| Echo/delay required on one particular word or section | **Lyrics** | I care about placement, not merely having echo somewhere in the song. |
| Arrangement event | **Lyrics** | Drop instruments here, build density here, strip back here, final dry vocal here. |
| Unusual compositional behaviour | **Lyrics** | Recursive motif, inherited layers, self-similar evolution, call-and-response rules, etc., especially when their sequence matters. |
| Genre / broad sonic world | **Style** | Deep house, Anatolian psych, art-pop, etc. describe the global sound. |
| Overall mood | **Style** | Dark, intimate, euphoric, nocturnal, aggressive, elegant. |
| General instrumentation | **Style** | “fuzzed saz, davul, bowed strings” if I want them available throughout but don't care exactly where each appears. |
| General vocal character | **Style** | Female contralto, raspy male lead, breathy intimate delivery. |
| Overall production aesthetic | **Style** | Analogue warmth, dry mix, tape saturation, spacious production. |
| General effect | **Style** | If I merely want “tape echo” somewhere and don't care where Suno places it. |
| Tempo / meter | **Style** | BPM, 9/8 Aksak, rhythmic identity as an overall song characteristic. |
| Exclusions | **Exclude Styles / Style controls** | What I do not want globally: EDM supersaws, trap hats, autotune, etc. |
| Remix strength / style influence / weirdness | **Dedicated controls** | These change how strongly Suno transforms or follows the supplied musical context; they are not composition instructions. |
| Length | **Dedicated length control**, where available | This is generation scope, not musical content. |

The simplest rule I would use as a Suno user is:

> **if i care where or when it happens, i put it in lyrics. if i care what the whole song generally sounds like but suno may decide where/how to realise it, i put it in style.**

For example, if I want **echo somewhere in the track**, Style:

`warm tape echo, distant vocal reflections`

If I specifically want the last word of the pre-chorus to fracture into echoes before the chorus, Lyrics:

```text
[pre-chorus]
...
aman

[the final "aman" leaves two smaller vocal reflections that remain underneath the next section]
```

And this is why our fractal work becomes interesting. **“self-similar evolving composition”** can sit in Style as a global identity, but the actual compositional architecture—

> seed appears → parent remains → descendant enters → environment changes → next descendant adapts

—belongs much more naturally in the **Lyrics/arrangement space**, because *placement and sequence are part of the composition itself*.

That is how I would use Suno if I were approaching the UI fresh.

Yes — this confirms the brand logic very clearly.

From the channel description itself, the successful formula is not just “Deep House.” It is a **positioned listening brand** built around four layers:

1. **Genre territory**
   Deep House, Vocal House, Chill House, Nu Disco.

2. **Sonic characteristics**
   Smooth basslines, emotional vocals, subtle melodies, sophisticated beats, atmospheric soundscapes.

3. **Use-case positioning**
   Late nights, night drives, studying, focus, relaxing, unwinding.

4. **Brand promise**
   **Clean. Emotional. Timeless.**

That last part is especially important. They are not marketing individual tracks first; they are marketing a **repeatable emotional environment**.

The numbers you pasted also make the strategy more interesting: **28.7K subscribers, 64 videos, 3.65M views**. That is roughly **57K views per upload on average**, which is strong for a channel of that size. So the relevant lesson is not merely “they have subscribers”; it is that the catalogue appears to produce repeatable consumption around a tightly defined identity.

For our project, I would preserve the same commercial architecture but change the sonic proposition completely.

Their brand equation is roughly:

> elegant electronic groove + emotional accessibility + lifestyle listening + consistent atmosphere

Ours should become:

> **Anatolian-rooted analogue groove + emotional intimacy + sophisticated nocturnal listening + distinctive recursive composition**

So we follow their **footsteps in positioning**, not their instrumentation.

The strongest overlap with your original brief is almost exact:

- “listeners who appreciate elegance, atmosphere, and timeless groove”
- “smooth basslines”
- “emotional vocals”
- “subtle melodies”
- “sophisticated beats”
- “late nights”
- “night drives”
- “relaxation”
- “focus”

Those were not incidental phrases in your prompt. They are the audience definition.

The main difference is our differentiator:

> **Their elegance comes from polished electronic deep-house vocabulary.**\
> **Our elegance should come from analogue/acoustic Anatolian vocabulary behaving with the same restraint, depth, and sophistication.**

That is the brand opportunity.

For example, where they use a soft synth pad, we use sustained saz/organ/room resonance. Where they use a deep-house sub, we use electric bass plus davul body. Where they use polished electronic percussion, we use darbuka, def and riq with controlled microtiming. Where they use reverb and delay atmospherics, we use spring reverb, tape echo, room microphones and re-amping.

And one more thing becomes obvious from their wording:

They repeatedly use **simple emotional language publicly**, while the actual production can be much more complex.

So our public-facing identity should also remain simple and elegant. We should not advertise the series as:

> “9/8 fractal recursive Anatolian analogue acoustic trap dub-techno fusion”

That is our **production architecture**.

The audience-facing brand should communicate something closer to:

> **deep, nocturnal, analogue, emotional, Anatolian, timeless**

while the complexity lives underneath.

That is probably the correct model for the entire series.

## The essential difference

**Gentleman is the umbrella artist/curator brand.**

**Deep & Elegant is the narrower product/format brand.**

That is the clearest way to understand the architecture.

| Dimension               | Gentleman                                              | Deep & Elegant                                                                |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Core identity           | Artist / DJ / tastemaker                               | Focused music-channel concept                                                 |
| Started                 | 2017                                                   | 2022                                                                          |
| Scale from your figures | 509K subs / 468 videos / 132M views                    | 117K subs / 180 videos / 30.6M views                                          |
| Brand promise           | Alternative, underground, atmospheric, original sounds | Deep/elegant atmosphere and coherent mixes                                    |
| Genre breadth           | Elegant Deep House, Electronic, Dub Techno, Downtempo  | More concentrated around deep/elegant house and adjacent underground variants |
| Personality             | Gentleman himself is central                           | The *sound world* is more central                                             |
| Role                    | Discovery, experimentation, artist identity            | Curated specialist destination                                                |
| Catalogue               | Broader creator/label ecosystem                        | Tracks specifically connected to GNTLMN                                       |

That distinction is strategically very sophisticated.

# 1. Gentleman is deliberately broader

Look carefully at the language you supplied:

> “not to chase general trends, but to provide his own unique sounds”

and:

> “atmospheric underground music of Elegant Deep House, Electronic, Dub Techno & Downtempo”

and:

> “diversified blend of vibes, rhythms and melodic textures”

Those phrases create permission for **variation**.

The Gentleman channel can move.

It can explore:

- deep house
- dub
- dub techno
- electronic
- downtempo
- lounge-adjacent material
- more experimental underground sounds

without breaking its identity.

Why?

Because the brand isn't defined by one precise genre.

The brand is:

> **Gentleman's taste.**

That is a classic **tastemaker model**.

The listener trusts the curator.

---

# 2. Deep & Elegant does almost the opposite

Its description is strikingly simple:

> “Its me Gentleman (DJ) This is my new channel, where you can listen to my music”

and:

> “All tracks are released under my label GNTLMN”

There is much less philosophical language.

That's important.

Deep & Elegant is less:

> “Here is what I believe about music.”

and more:

> **“Here is the product.”**

The channel launched later, in October 2022, and contemporary descriptions called it specifically a **new channel** created by Gentleman. Its early programming already included *Deep House Mix*, *Deep & Dub*, *Underground Vibes*, *Deep City Groove*, etc.

That strongly suggests deliberate segmentation rather than accidental duplication.

---

# 3. Why create Deep & Elegant when Gentleman already had hundreds of thousands of followers?

This is probably the most useful question for **our** project.

Because a broad successful brand eventually faces a problem:

### Audience expectation becomes heterogeneous.

Someone subscribed for Dub Techno.

Another person subscribed for Deep House.

Another wants Downtempo.

Another follows Gentleman himself.

That gives the flagship breadth, but reduces **predictability**.

Deep & Elegant fixes that.

It tells the audience:

> **Here is one clearly defined lane.**

That makes each upload easier to understand algorithmically and psychologically.

You don't have to ask:

> “What is Gentleman uploading today?”

You already know roughly what emotional territory **Deep & Elegant** will occupy.

That is incredibly useful for YouTube.

---

# 4. Gentleman = creator-led brand

The bigger channel's identity repeatedly foregrounds:

**Gentleman's philosophy**\
**Gentleman's taste**\
**Gentleman's selections**\
**Gentleman's mixes**

Even individual mix titles do this.

For example, preserved catalogue listings include:

- *Gentleman - Summer Deep House Mix*
- *Gentleman - Deep Trip*
- *Gentleman - To All The Ladies*
- *Gentleman - Quarantine*
- *Deepest Vibes [Gentleman 'Old' Selection]*

This is personality-based curation.

The implicit promise is:

> **I trust this DJ to choose good music.**

# 5. Deep & Elegant = environment-led brand

Here, the title architecture increasingly foregrounds:

**Deep**\
**Elegant**\
**Underground**\
**City**\
**Luxury**\
**Dub**\
**Vibes**

rather than simply “Gentleman.”

The implied promise changes to:

> **I want to enter this sonic environment.**

This matters enormously for passive listening.

A user doesn't necessarily care who produced every record.

They care that clicking:

**Deep & Elegant**

gives them:

**deep + elegant + atmospheric + consistent**

music.

It becomes a **destination** rather than merely an artist channel.

Yes. We can turn what we have been doing informally into a **repeatable Suno Style Discovery Protocol**.

The purpose is **not initially to make the final song**. It is to discover **Suno's own vocabulary and interpretation for unfamiliar musical ideas**.

### Method for every test

For each item below:

1. Put only the relevant description in the **Lyrics** field, inside square brackets.
2. Describe **what it should sound/feel like first**.
3. Then describe the unusual construction or musical behaviour.
4. Press **Create Style / generate style description**.
5. Copy Suno's generated Style text exactly.
6. Compare:
   - what it preserved,
   - what it renamed,
   - what it simplified,
   - what familiar instrument/style it substituted,
   - what new terminology it introduced,
   - what it ignored.
7. When useful, repeat the same test after generating/remixing audio and compare whether Suno's Style description becomes more specific.
8. Keep successful Suno terminology for our eventual **new-genre vocabulary**, without automatically accepting inaccurate substitutions.

## Merged exploration list

1. **Core new sound identity**

   `[CORE SOUND IDENTITY: dark, warm, late-night, deep, elegant, raw, intimate, woody, dusty, magnetic, physical, human; underground house-like hypnotic repetition carried by Anatolian rhythmic movement rather than standard electronic production]`

   Explore what Suno calls the overall sound before we give it a genre name.

2. **9/8 Aksak as an audible feeling**

   `[9/8 AKSAK SOUND: smooth rolling asymmetry, gentle pull, stretch and return, circular bodily movement, hypnotic rather than mathematically complex, uneven without sounding broken]`

   Look for Suno terms such as *sway, lilt, rolling pulse, elastic groove, circular feel,* etc.

3. **Specific 2+2+2+3 Aksak behaviour**

   `[AKSAK RHYTHMIC MOVEMENT: 9/8 grouped 2+2+2+3, three equal-feeling movements followed by a longer final movement before returning to the beginning, steady → steady → steady → stretch → return]`

   Determine how Suno describes the final 3-pulse cell.

4. **House movement without conventional 4/4**

   `[ASYMMETRICAL HOUSE PULSE: bodily late-night house-like repetition inside continuous 9/8, four grounded low-frequency anchors but an extended final return, never straight 4/4]`

   We want to discover Suno's language for the **four-on-the-floor illusion without four-on-the-floor meter**.

5. **Davul anchor system**

   `[DAVUL GROOVE: deep acoustic davul anchors on pulses 1, 3, 5 and 7, creating four strong physical points inside the 9/8 cycle]`

   See whether Suno says *kick, four anchors, house pulse, grounded beat, acoustic bass drum,* etc.

6. **Pulse-9 gravitational low end**

   `[END-OF-CYCLE LOW-END BLOOM: after the four main davul anchors, one very deep tuned davul resonance on pulse 9 creates a stretched gravitational pull into the next downbeat]`

   This deserves its own test because Suno already produced useful language such as **“end-of-cycle bloom”** and **“gravitational momentum.”**

7. **Acoustic house low end without synth bass**

   `[ACOUSTIC LOW-END SYSTEM: deep rounded house-scale physical weight created from tuned davul impact, wooden-body resonance, room energy and analogue saturation; breathing space between hits rather than constant synthetic sub tone]`

   Explore how Suno describes **acoustic sub-like weight**.

8. **Darbuka functioning as house backbeat**

   `[DARBUKA BACKBEAT SOUND: dry, sharp, close, short and damped darbuka strikes functioning like compact house backbeats while remaining clearly tactile hand-played skin percussion]`

   Discover whether Suno can retain both **instrument identity** and **house function**.

9. **Def and riq functioning as house hats/shakers**

   `[DEF AND RIQ GROOVE: fine shimmering continuous upper-percussion movement surrounding the davul, smooth like elegant house shakers and hi-hats but clearly produced by fingers, skins and metal jingles]`

   This produced strong results already and should be isolated.

   `[FINAL THREE-PULSE PERCUSSION MOVEMENT: def and riq remain hypnotically repetitive but make a subtle additional movement inside the final three pulses, revealing the Aksak lilt without breaking the trance]`

   Explore Suno's terminology for this micro-rhythmic behaviour.

   `[HUMAN RHYTHMIC FEEL: tiny timing differences, dynamic variation, hand-played accents, skin resonance and natural microtiming; hypnotically stable but never mechanically quantised]`

   See what terms Suno associates with this: *loose, organic, humanized, live, swung,* etc.
